economics.title: Saturday shift and a free course
economics.context: Lea has one free Saturday afternoon. She can work a paid shift that earns €80, or she can attend a revision course that charges no fee. She takes the shift. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The opportunity cost of taking the shift is the revision she gives up, not the €80 she receives.
Because the revision course charges no fee, choosing the course would have an opportunity cost of zero.
Scarcity is absent, because Lea has only two options and scarcity requires a long list of alternatives.
The €80 wage is the opportunity cost of taking the shift.
If Lea had attended the course instead, part of the opportunity cost would be the €80 she did not earn.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative given up. Lea used the afternoon on the shift, so what she sacrificed is the revision course. The €80 is what the chosen option pays her; it is not the thing she lost by choosing it.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A zero ticket price does not make the opportunity cost zero. If Lea takes the free course, she gives up the shift and the €80 that shift would have paid. The forgone earning is a real cost even though the classroom itself charges nothing.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Scarcity is already present when one afternoon cannot be spent twice. Two options are enough: the same hours cannot be both a shift and a revision class. A long menu is not required before a choice becomes an economic choice.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The €80 is the benefit of the option she actually took. Opportunity cost names the alternative left behind, which here is the revision course. Calling the wage itself the opportunity cost swaps the payoff of the choice with the sacrifice of the choice.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Had she sat the course, she would not have earned the €80. That lost pay is the leading alternative given up, so it belongs in the opportunity cost of the course. The fact that the course fee is zero does not erase the wage she turned down.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: Bus fares, petrol, and incomes
economics.context: A city bus company studies its own fare, the price of petrol, household incomes, and a new advertising campaign for bus travel. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A higher price of petrol, treated as a substitute for many bus trips, tends to shift the demand curve for bus rides to the right.
A cut in the bus fare, with the demand curve unchanged, is a movement along that demand curve.
If bus travel is an inferior good for a group of households, a rise in their incomes shifts their demand for bus rides to the left.
An advertising campaign that makes bus travel more attractive shifts the supply curve of bus rides, not the demand curve.
Once demand shifts, the old equilibrium price and quantity remain the correct market outcome because the supply curve did not move.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Petrol and the bus compete for the same journeys. When driving becomes more expensive, some travellers switch toward the bus at every given fare. That is a rightward shift of bus demand, caused by the price of a substitute, not by the bus company’s own fare.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The fare is the own price of a bus ride. Changing that price, while tastes, incomes, and related prices stay put, slides quantity along the existing demand curve. It does not draw a new demand curve.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For an inferior good, higher income means buyers want less of it at each price. If the bus plays that role for these households, their demand curve shifts left when incomes rise. Normal-good logic would shift demand the other way, and that logic does not apply once the good is inferior.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Advertising that makes bus travel more desirable changes how many rides people want at each fare. That is a demand shift. Supply would move if the company’s costs or capacity changed, which this campaign does not do.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A demand shift meets the same supply curve at a different point. Both the equilibrium fare and the equilibrium number of rides generally change. Leaving the old intersection in place would ignore the new willingness to ride.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Vineyard, bottling, and EU size
economics.context: A vineyard harvests grapes. A winery ferments and bottles wine. A shop sells the finished bottles to households. Separately, a firm employs 8 people, has annual turnover of €1.5 million, and reports a balance-sheet total of €2.4 million. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Harvesting grapes is primary production, bottling the wine is secondary production, and selling the bottles in the shop is a tertiary activity.
The shop belongs to the secondary sector because it handles a physical good rather than a service.
The firm with 8 employees and turnover of €1.5 million can still be a micro-enterprise even though the balance-sheet total is €2.4 million.
Fewer than 10 employees is enough, by itself, for micro status even when both turnover and the balance-sheet total are above €2 million.
Bottling wine remains a purely primary activity because the grapes were grown on a farm.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Primary production takes something from nature, which is what the harvest does. Secondary production transforms that material; fermenting and bottling are manufacturing. Selling the finished bottles to households is trade, a tertiary activity. Each stage is classified by what is done at that stage, not by the product’s origin.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The shop does not manufacture the wine. It distributes a finished good to customers, which is tertiary trade. Handling a physical object does not turn retail into secondary production. The bottling plant is the secondary stage; the counter is not.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Micro status needs fewer than 10 employees and at least one of the two financial ceilings. Eight employees meet the staff test. Turnover of €1.5 million is not above €2 million, so the turnover ceiling is met even though the balance-sheet total of €2.4 million is over its own ceiling. One financial ceiling is enough.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Staff below ten is only half of the test. If turnover is above €2 million and the balance-sheet total is also above €2 million, neither financial ceiling is met. The firm then fails micro status despite the small payroll. Headcount does not override both financial misses at once.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Growing the grapes is primary. Turning those grapes into bottled wine is a manufacturing step, so it is secondary. The farm origin of the input does not keep the processing stage in the primary sector.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Sole trader, partnership, and corporation
economics.context: Compare a sole trader, a general partnership, and a corporation whose shares can be resold on a stock exchange. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A sole trader is not a separate legal person from the owner, so business creditors can pursue the owner’s private assets.
Shareholders of a corporation are normally liable for company debts only up to the capital they agreed to contribute.
Shareholders of a corporation must also be its day-to-day managers.
A general partner’s liability for partnership debts is limited to that partner’s percentage share of the profits.
After the shares have already been issued, a rise in their stock-exchange price pays new cash into the corporation equal to that gain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A sole trader and the business are the same legal person. There is no corporate shell between the shop’s debts and the owner. If the business cannot pay, creditors can reach private assets, which is what unlimited liability means here.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A corporation is a legal person of its own. Shareholders generally risk only the capital they subscribed. Company debts are claims on the company, not an open claim on each shareholder’s house or savings beyond that contribution.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Ownership and management are separate jobs in a corporation. Shareholders can appoint directors and hire managers, then stay out of daily operations. Nothing in the corporate form forces every owner to run the working day.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A profit percentage divides gains. It does not cap a general partner’s liability at that same percentage of the debts. General partners remain unlimitedly liable, so a creditor can pursue one of them for more than that partner’s profit share.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Once the shares are in circulation, a higher market price is a gain for the shareholders who sell to each other. The corporation already received its money at issue. Later trading does not send a matching cash amount into the company.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Machine finance and a short inventory gap
economics.context: A manufacturer needs funds for a machine that will be used for eight years, and separate funds for a three-month build-up of inventory. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Retained earnings are an internal source of equity finance.
A bank overdraft used for the inventory build-up is external short-term debt.
A long-term loan is a closer match for the eight-year machine than an overdraft that the bank can withdraw at short notice.
Trade credit from suppliers is equity finance, because suppliers do not always charge a stated interest rate.
Cash raised by issuing new shares to outside investors is internal finance, because the money ends up in the firm’s bank account.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Retained earnings are profits the owners leave in the business instead of taking them out. No new lender and no new shareholder is involved, so the finance is internal, and it increases equity rather than debt.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The bank is an outsider, so an overdraft is external finance. It has to be repaid and it is designed for a short horizon, which fits a three-month inventory bulge better than a permanent capital injection. That makes it short-term debt, not equity.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The machine earns its keep over eight years. Funding it with a facility the bank can call quickly leaves the firm exposed when the asset is still in use. A long-term loan lines the repayment period up with the asset’s life more closely than an overdraft does.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Trade credit is a debt to suppliers: the firm has received goods and still owes the invoice. Missing a stated interest rate does not turn that payable into ownership capital. Equity comes from owners, not from a postponed supplier bill.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

New shares sold to outside investors bring in cash from people who were not already financing the firm this way. The cash sitting in the bank account does not make the source internal. Issuing shares to outsiders is external equity.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Sandwich price cut and the marketing mix
economics.context: A café cuts the price of a sandwich from €8 to €6. Weekly sales rise from 200 to 280 sandwiches. Measure elasticity from the initial price and the initial quantity. In the same week the café pays for Instagram posts about the sandwich and moves the pickup counter closer to the entrance. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Demand is elastic over this change, because the percentage increase in quantity is larger than the percentage fall in price.
The magnitude of elasticity, measured from the initial point, is about 0.6, so demand is inelastic.
Weekly revenue from the sandwich is higher after the price cut than before it.
The Instagram posts are a place decision, and moving the pickup counter is a promotion decision.
The elasticity calculated from this one week must equal the long-run elasticity of the same sandwich.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Quantity rises from 200 to 280, which is 80/200 = 40%. Price falls from €8 to €6, which is 2/8 = 25%. The quantity response is larger than the price response, so demand is elastic over this change.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

From the initial point the magnitude is 40% divided by 25%, which is 1.6, not 0.6. A figure above 1 means elastic demand. The claim both miscalculates the ratio and then attaches the wrong label.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Revenue before the cut is 8 × 200 = €1,600. Revenue after the cut is 6 × 280 = €1,680. The extra sandwiches more than replace the lower price, which is what elastic demand leads you to expect for a price cut.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Instagram posts tell customers about the sandwich, so they are promotion. Moving the counter changes where the customer collects the product, so it is place. The statement swaps the two mix elements.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

One week shows a short-run response. Over a longer period customers can change habits, find other cafés, or treat the new price as normal, so long-run elasticity can differ. Nothing in this week’s count forces the two horizons to match.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Liquidity From the Balance Sheet 9
economics.context:
Consider the following balance sheet (in € thousands) for a business whose identity is not disclosed.

| € in thousands | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| **ASSETS** | |
| Buildings | 409 |
| Machinery | 265 |
| Office equipment | 40 |
| Patents, trademarks and licences | 72 |
| Inventory | 201 |
| Trade receivables | 163 |
| Cash and cash equivalents | 42 |
| Total assets | **1192** |
| **EQUITY** | |
| Share capital | 183 |
| Retained earnings | 444 |
| Total equity | **627** |
| **LIABILITIES** | |
| Long-term bank loan | 328 |
| Bonds payable | 78 |
| Trade payables | 101 |
| Bank overdraft | 58 |
| Total liabilities | **565** |
| Total equity and liabilities | **1192** |

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Owner's equity is the portion of assets financed by bank loans and trade creditors.
The current ratio exceeds 1.47.
Working capital of €247 thousand is positive on this balance sheet.
After excluding inventory, the remaining current assets still cover current liabilities more than 0.64 times over.
The current ratio is below 0.72.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Owner's equity is the residual claim after liabilities, not the slice financed by banks or trade creditors. Loans and trade payables sit in the liabilities block.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Current assets are inventory, trade receivables and cash. Current liabilities are trade payables and the bank overdraft.

$$
201 + 163 + 42 = 406
$$

$$
101 + 58 = 159
$$

$$
\dfrac{406}{159} \approx 2.55
$$

$$
2.55 > 1.47
$$

The current ratio is about $2.55$, above $1.47$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities:

$$
406 - 159 = 247
$$

EUR $247$ thousand is positive, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Drop inventory from current assets, then compare with the same current liabilities:

$$
406 - 201 = 205
$$

$$
\dfrac{205}{159} \approx 1.29
$$

$$
1.29 > 0.64
$$

The quick cover is about $1.29$ times, above $0.64$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The current ratio from letter B is about $2.55$:

$$
2.55 > 0.72
$$

A ratio of about $2.55$ is not below $0.72$.

So the statement is False.
economics.solution_overview: Current assets are inventory, trade receivables and cash. Current liabilities are trade payables and the bank overdraft. Working capital is CA − CL. The current ratio is CA ÷ CL. The quick cover drops inventory before dividing by CL.

economics.title: Profit and Loss Over Two Years 2
economics.context:
Consider the following two-year statement of profit and loss (in € thousands) for a business whose identity is not disclosed.

| Item (€ thousands) | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 1055 | 1281 |
| Cost of sales | (644) | (787) |
| Gross profit | 411 | 494 |
| Distribution costs | (35) | (49) |
| General and administrative costs | (38) | (48) |
| Other operating result | 4 | 3 |
| Operating result | 342 | 400 |
| Finance costs | (22) | (26) |
| Finance costs – net | (19) | (22) |
| Profit before tax | 323 | 378 |
| Income taxes | (69) | (79) |
| Profit for the year | 254 | 299 |

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Purchase of a plant, machinery or other long-term asset for cash is classified as cash flow from investing activities.
The gross profit margin, gross profit taken as a share of revenue, is more than 4.8 percentage points higher in Year 2 than in Year 1.
Revenue grew by more than 19.8% between Year 1 and Year 2.
The operating result grew by more than 37.5% between Year 1 and Year 2.
The operating result covers finance costs more than 9.14 times over in Year 1.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Cash spent on plant, machinery or another long-term asset is an investing outflow. It is not an operating cash flow.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue.

$$
\dfrac{411}{1055} \approx 0.390 = 39.0\%
$$

$$
\dfrac{494}{1281} \approx 0.386 = 38.6\%
$$

$$
38.6 - 39.0 = -0.4
$$

Year 2 is about $0.4$ percentage points lower, not more than $4.8$ points higher.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Revenue growth is the change divided by Year 1:

$$
\dfrac{1281 - 1055}{1055} = \dfrac{226}{1055} \approx 0.214 = 21.4\%
$$

$$
21.4\% > 19.8\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Operating-result growth:

$$
\dfrac{400 - 342}{342} = \dfrac{58}{342} \approx 0.170 = 17.0\%
$$

$$
17.0\% \ngtr 37.5\%
$$

Growth is about $17\%$, not above $37.5\%$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Interest cover in Year 1 is operating result divided by finance costs:

$$
\dfrac{342}{22} \approx 15.55
$$

$$
15.55 > 9.14
$$

The operating result covers finance costs about $15.5$ times, above $9.14$.

So the statement is True.
economics.solution_overview: Gross margin is gross profit ÷ revenue. Growth is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1. Interest cover in Year 1 is operating result ÷ finance costs. A cash purchase of plant is an investing cash flow.

economics.title: Cash Flow Statement Over Two Years 6
economics.context:
Consider the following two-year cash flow statement extract (in € thousands) for a business whose identity is not disclosed.

| Item (€ thousands) | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cash flow from operating activities | 314 | 359 |
| Cash flow from investing activities | (347) | (299) |
| Dividends paid | (39) | (56) |
| Proceeds from new borrowing | 60 | 50 |
| Cash flow from financing activities | 21 | (6) |

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A negative cash flow from investing activities always proves the business is in financial trouble.
Cash flow from operating activities grew by more than 13.7% from Year 1 to Year 2.
Cash flow from financing activities was higher in Year 2 than in Year 1.
The increase in dividends paid from Year 1 to Year 2 was proportionally smaller than the increase in cash flow from operating activities.
Paying dividends is classified as an investing cash outflow because it uses cash belonging to shareholders.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A negative investing cash flow often means the firm bought long-term assets. That can be expansion, not distress. The sign alone does not prove financial trouble.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Operating cash flow growth:

$$
\dfrac{359 - 314}{314} = \dfrac{45}{314} \approx 0.143 = 14.3\%
$$

$$
14.3\% > 13.7\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Financing cash flow is $21$ in Year 1 and $-6$ in Year 2.

$$
-6 < 21
$$

Year 2 is lower, not higher.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Dividend growth versus operating-cash growth:

$$
\dfrac{56 - 39}{39} = \dfrac{17}{39} \approx 43.6\%
$$

$$
\dfrac{45}{314} \approx 14.3\%
$$

$$
43.6\% > 14.3\%
$$

The dividend increase is proportionally larger, not smaller.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Dividends paid to owners are a financing outflow. They are not classified as investing just because the cash belongs to shareholders.

So the statement is False.
economics.solution_overview: Compare each cash-flow heading year on year. Growth is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1. Dividends paid belong to financing, not investing. A negative investing total can be asset purchases rather than distress.

3.91\% \nless 3\%

The yield is about $3.91\%$, not below $3\%$.
