math.title: Five mixed hard equations — no shortcuts
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. Five independent mixed equations. The five claims deliberately use different judgment styles — candidate survival, root count, size comparison, threshold, and sign/location — so do not expect the same wording twice.
statements: Squaring twice for $\sqrt{3x+7}+\sqrt{x+1}=4$ produces two real candidates, and both of them survive domain checks and back-substitution.
After discarding the poles $x=1$ and $x=-4$, the equation $\dfrac{x+2}{x-1}+\dfrac{2x-3}{x+4}=\dfrac{3x^{2}+5x-2}{(x-1)(x+4)}$ reduces to a linear condition with exactly one surviving real root.
Every real solution of $|x^{2}-6x+5|=3x-4$ is strictly larger than $3$.
Every domain-legal real solution of $\log_{2}(x-1)+\log_{2}(x+3)=\log_{2}(3x+5)$ is strictly larger than $4$.
The equation $\sqrt{x+3}+|x-1|=4$ has at least one negative real solution and at least one real solution greater than $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Domain of both radicals: $x\ge -1$. Isolate and keep the right-hand side nonnegative:

$$
\sqrt{3x+7}=4-\sqrt{x+1},\qquad 4-\sqrt{x+1}\ge 0\implies x\le 15
$$

Square once:

$$
3x+7=16-8\sqrt{x+1}+(x+1)\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 2x-10=-8\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
5-x=4\sqrt{x+1}
$$

(the sign of $5-x$ must stay nonnegative, so $x\le 5$). Square again:

$$
(5-x)^{2}=16(x+1)\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x^{2}-26x+9=0
$$

$$
x=13\pm 4\sqrt{10}
$$

The larger root $13+4\sqrt{10}\approx 25.6$ lies outside the domain window. Only the smaller root $13-4\sqrt{10}\approx 0.35$ survives back-substitution into the original equation. Squaring twice therefore produces two real candidates, but only one of them survives. The claim that both survive is false.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Poles $x=1$ and $x=-4$ are excluded. Clearing the common denominator $(x-1)(x+4)$ cancels the quadratic terms and leaves the linear condition

$$
x+11=5x-2\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 4x=13\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

The value $\tfrac{13}{4}$ is neither pole, so exactly one real root survives.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The right-hand side forces $3x-4\ge 0$, i.e. $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$. Split $|x^{2}-6x+5|$ at the roots of $x^{2}-6x+5=(x-1)(x-5)$.

On the branch where $x^{2}-6x+5\ge 0$ (outside $[1,5]$) one admissible survivor is near $x\approx 7.85$. On the branch inside $(1,5)$ where the quadratic is negative, another survivor appears near $x\approx 2.62$.

The smaller root $2.62$ is strictly less than $3$. Therefore it is false that every real solution exceeds $3$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Domain: $x>1$ (and $3x+5>0$, automatic there). Combine logs:

$$
\log_{2}\bigl((x-1)(x+3)\bigr)=\log_{2}(3x+5)
$$

so $(x-1)(x+3)=3x+5$, which rearranges to

$$
x^{2}-2x-8=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x=1\pm\sqrt{9}\quad\text{(check)}\quad x=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 3.37
$$

(the negative branch is outside the domain). The unique legal root is about $3.37$, which is not strictly larger than $4$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Split at the kink $x=1$ of $|x-1|$.

**Case $x\ge 1$.** The equation is $\sqrt{x+3}+(x-1)=4$, i.e. $\sqrt{x+3}=5-x$ with $x\le 5$. Squaring:

$$
x+3=(5-x)^{2}=25-10x+x^{2}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x^{2}-11x+22=0
$$

$$
x=\dfrac{11\pm\sqrt{33}}{2}
$$

The larger candidate $\dfrac{11+\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 8.37$ fails $x\le 5$. The smaller $\dfrac{11-\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 2.63$ lies in $[1,5]$ and survives — a root greater than $2$.

**Case $-3\le x<1$.** Now $\sqrt{x+3}+(1-x)=4$, i.e. $\sqrt{x+3}=3+x$. At $x=-2$:

$$
\sqrt{1}+(1-(-2))=1+3=4
$$

so $x=-2$ is a negative real solution.

Both required locations appear.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Five independent mixed equations. Work each letter from its own domain restrictions; none of the five collapses by a one-line sum/product identity.

**Part 1: Radical equation $\sqrt{3x+7}+\sqrt{x+1}=4$.**

Domain of both radicals:

$$
3x+7\ge 0\implies x\ge -\frac{7}{3}
$$

$$
x+1\ge 0\implies x\ge -1
$$

so overall $x\ge -1$. Isolate and keep the right-hand side nonnegative:

$$
\sqrt{3x+7}=4-\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
4-\sqrt{x+1}\ge 0\implies x\le 15
$$

Square once, rearrange, and square again to reach

$$
(5-x)^{2}=16(x+1)
$$

$$
x^{2}-26x+9=0
$$

$$
x=13\pm 4\sqrt{10}
$$

Only the smaller root lies in $[-1,5]$ and survives back-substitution.

**Part 2: Rational identity.**

Clear the common denominator $(x-1)(x+4)$ (poles excluded). After expansion the quadratic terms cancel and the linear condition

$$
x+11=5x-2
$$

$$
4x=13
$$

$$
x=\frac{13}{4}
$$

survives.

**Part 3: Absolute value, logs, and mixed radical.**

Absolute-value cases under $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$ produce survivors near $7.85$ and $2.62$; logs on $x>1$ yield the unique survivor $(1+\sqrt{33})/2\approx 3.37$; splitting $\sqrt{x+3}+|x-1|=4$ at $x=1$ produces negative roots and a root larger than $2$.

math.title: Print-shop mix — two unknowns, five traps
math.context:
A print shop sells only mono pages and colour pages. In one batch it printed a total of $180$ pages and booked revenue EUR 8100. Mono sells at EUR 35 each and colour at EUR 55 each:
$$
m+c=180,\qquad 35m+55c=8100.
$$
The unique baseline solution is the factual starting point. Decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The unique baseline solution is $(m,c)=(90,90)$.
If the colour price had been EUR 60 instead of EUR 55, with the same count $m+c=180$ and the same revenue EUR 8100, then $c$ would have fallen below $75$.
If management had printed $15$ fewer mono pages and $15$ more colour pages than the baseline, revenue would have risen by exactly EUR 300.
If total pages stayed $180$ but the revenue target rose to EUR 10000 at the same prices, no nonnegative solution $(m,c)$ would exist, because an all-colour batch only reaches EUR 9900.
If prices stayed EUR 35 and EUR 55 but the shop printed the swapped mix $(120,60)$ instead of the baseline $(90,90)$, revenue would still be EUR 8100.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Substitute $m=180-c$ into the revenue equation:

$$
35(180-c)+55c=8100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 6300+20c=8100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad c=90
$$

$$
m=180-90=90
$$

So the unique baseline is $(m,c)=(90,90)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Replace the colour price by EUR $60$, keep $m+c=180$ and revenue $8100$:

$$
35(180-c)+60c=8100
$$

$$
6300-35c+60c=8100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 25c=1800\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad c=72
$$

$$
72<75
$$

Colour volume falls to $72$, below $75$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Baseline is $(90,90)$. The shifted mix is $(75,105)$:

$$
35\cdot 75+55\cdot 105=2625+5775=8400
$$

$$
8400-8100=300
$$

Revenue rises by exactly EUR $300$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

An all-colour batch of $180$ pages yields

$$
55\cdot 180=9900
$$

which is already below the EUR $10000$ target. Any mix with some mono pages (cheaper) yields even less. No nonnegative solution reaches $10000$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At the swapped mix $(120,60)$:

$$
35\cdot 120+55\cdot 60=4200+3300=7500\neq 8100
$$

Revenue falls to EUR $7500$, not $8100$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Hard mixed inequalities — varied interval claims
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. All five letters are inequalities, but the claims are worded differently on purpose: absence of counterexamples, existence inside an open interval, existence on a closed interval, containment of a segment, and nonempty intersection.
statements: No point of the interval $[1,4]$ violates $|x^{2}-5x+4|+|2x-3|\le x+6$.
The inequality $\sqrt{2x+5}+|x-2|\le 4$ admits at least one solution in the open interval $(1,2)$.
There exists some $x\in[0,1]$ for which $\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}\ge 1$.
The solution set of $\dfrac{|x|}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2$ contains every point of $[0,1]$.
The inequality $\dfrac{|2x-5|}{|x+1|}+|x-2|\le 4$ has nonempty intersection with the interval $[-4,-2]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $[1,4]$ the critical points of $|x^{2}-5x+4|+|2x-3|$ are $x=1$, $x=\tfrac{3}{2}$, and $x=4$.

**Piece $[1,\tfrac{3}{2}]$.** Here $x^{2}-5x+4\le 0$ and $2x-3\le 0$, so the inequality becomes

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(3-2x)\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+3x-1\le x+6\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 0\le x^{2}-2x+7
$$

Discriminant $4-28=-24<0$, so $x^{2}-2x+7>0$ everywhere on this piece.

**Piece $[\tfrac{3}{2},4]$.** Now $2x-3\ge 0$ and still $x^{2}-5x+4\le 0$ until $x=4$, giving

$$
0\le x^{2}-6x+13
$$

Discriminant $36-52=-16<0$, again always true.

No point of $[1,4]$ violates the inequality.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Domain needs $x\ge -\tfrac{5}{2}$. Test the interior point $x=\tfrac{3}{2}\in(1,2)$:

$$
\sqrt{2\cdot\tfrac{3}{2}+5}+\bigl|\tfrac{3}{2}-2\bigr|=\sqrt{8}+\tfrac{1}{2}=2\sqrt{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\approx 3.328\le 4
$$

A witness inside $(1,2)$ exists.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Away from the poles of the rational expression, cancelling the common factor $x-2$ reduces $\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}\ge 1$ to $-\dfrac{4}{x+1}\ge 0$, i.e. $x<-1$. The closed interval $[0,1]$ lies entirely outside that half-line, so no point of $[0,1]$ satisfies the inequality.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

On $[0,1]$ one has $\dfrac{|x|}{x+3}=\dfrac{x}{x+3}$ and $\sqrt{x+1}$, both increasing, so the left-hand side is increasing. Its maximum on the segment is at $x=1$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{4}+\sqrt{2}\approx 0.25+1.414=1.664\le 2
$$

Every point of $[0,1]$ therefore satisfies the inequality.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

On $[-4,-2]$ both $|2x-5|=5-2x$ and $|x+1|=-(x+1)$ and $|x-2|=2-x$ (since $x\le -2<2$). The left-hand side becomes

$$
\dfrac{5-2x}{-(x+1)}+(2-x)=\dfrac{5-2x}{-x-1}+2-x
$$

At the midpoint $x=-3$:

$$
\dfrac{5-2(-3)}{-(-3)-1}+2-(-3)=\dfrac{11}{2}+5=10.5>4
$$

At the endpoints $x=-4$ and $x=-2$ the value is likewise strictly above $4$. The expression stays larger than $4$ on the whole interval, so the intersection with $[-4,-2]$ is empty.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Five mixed inequalities with deliberately varied claim styles: no-counterexample, existence in an open interval, existence on a closed interval, segment containment, and nonempty intersection.

**Part 1: Absolute-value inequality on $[1,4]$.**

Critical points of $|x^{2}-5x+4|+|2x-3|\le x+6$ on $[1,4]$ are $x=1$, $x=\tfrac{3}{2}$, and $x=4$. On $[1,\tfrac{3}{2}]$:

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(3-2x)\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+5x-4+3-2x\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+3x-1\le x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-2x+7
$$

Discriminant of $x^{2}-2x+7$:

$$
4-28=-24<0
$$

so the quadratic is always positive. On $[\tfrac{3}{2},4]$:

$$
0\le x^{2}-6x+13
$$

$$
36-52=-16<0
$$

again always positive. No counterexample on $[1,4]$.

**Part 2: Existence checks.**

For $\sqrt{2x+5}+|x-2|\le 4$, domain $x\ge -\tfrac{5}{2}$. Interior test at $x=\tfrac{3}{2}\in(1,2)$:

$$
\sqrt{8}+\tfrac{1}{2}=2\sqrt{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\approx 3.328\le 4
$$

witnesses existence.

For the rational inequality, cancel $x-2$ away from the poles to obtain $-4/(x+1)\ge 0$, i.e. $x<-1$; the segment $[0,1]$ lies entirely outside that half-line.

**Part 3: Containment and empty intersection.**

On $[0,1]$ the left-hand side of $\dfrac{|x|}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2$ is increasing and its maximum at $x=1$ is still $\le 2$. On $[-4,-2]$ the expression $\dfrac{|2x-5|}{|x+1|}+|x-2|$ stays larger than $4$ (e.g. $10.5$ at $x=-3$).

math.title: Parametric quadratic family — critical cases
math.context:
For each real parameter $k$, define
$$
g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4).
$$
Decide whether each claim about this family is true or false.
statements: For every real $k$, the equation $g_k(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots.
The axis of symmetry of $y=g_k(x)$ is $x=k+\tfrac12$ for every $k$.
If $k=2$, then the roots are $x=1$ and $x=5$.
There exists a real $k$ for which both roots are equal to $0$.
The vertex $y$-coordinate equals $-\dfrac{17}{4}$ when $k=0$.
math.solution_overview:
A one-parameter quadratic family. Read the axis, discriminant, and vertex from the coefficients; then specialise $k$ only when a letter asks for it.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4)
$$

Write the standard coefficients:

$$
a=1
$$

$$
B=2k+1
$$

$$
C=k^{2}-4
$$

**Part 2: Axis and discriminant.**

Axis of symmetry:

$$
x=\frac{B}{2a}=\frac{2k+1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{2k+1}{2}=k+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Discriminant expansion:

$$
\Delta=(2k+1)^{2}-4(k^{2}-4)
$$

$$
(2k+1)^{2}=4k^{2}+4k+1
$$

$$
4(k^{2}-4)=4k^{2}-16
$$

$$
\Delta=4k^{2}+4k+1-(4k^{2}-16)
$$

$$
\Delta=4k^{2}+4k+1-4k^{2}+16
$$

$$
\Delta=4k+17
$$

**Part 3: Vertex $y$-value and special cases.**

For a monic quadratic the vertex height is $-\Delta/4$:

$$
g_k\Bigl(k+\tfrac12\Bigr)=-\frac{\Delta}{4}=-\frac{4k+17}{4}
$$

At $k=0$:

$$
\Delta=17
$$

$$
-\frac{17}{4}
$$

At $k=2$:

$$
g_2(x)=x^{2}-5x=x(x-5)
$$

roots $0$ and $5$. A double root at $0$ would need both $C=0$ and $B=0$, which force incompatible values of $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Expand the discriminant of $g_k$:

$$
\Delta=(2k+1)^{2}-4(k^{2}-4)=4k^{2}+4k+1-4k^{2}+16=4k+17
$$

For $k=-5$:

$$
\Delta=4(-5)+17=-3<0
$$

so $g_{-5}(x)=0$ has no real roots. The claim that every real $k$ yields two distinct real roots fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

For $g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4)$ the axis is

$$
x=\dfrac{2k+1}{2}=k+\tfrac{1}{2}
$$

for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

At $k=2$:

$$
g_2(x)=x^{2}-5x+(4-4)=x^{2}-5x=x(x-5)
$$

The roots are $x=0$ and $x=5$, not $x=1$ and $x=5$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A double root at $0$ would require the constant term and the linear coefficient both to vanish:

$$
k^{2}-4=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad 2k+1=0
$$

The second forces $k=-\tfrac{1}{2}$, but then $k^{2}-4=\tfrac{1}{4}-4\neq 0$. No such real $k$ exists.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

At $k=0$, $\Delta=17$. For a monic quadratic the vertex height is $-\Delta/4$:

$$
g_0\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigr)=-\dfrac{17}{4}
$$

So the statement is True.

math.title: Courier tariff — affine day/night word problem
math.context: A courier charges a daytime base fee of EUR 12 plus EUR 0.8 per kilometre. Night runs use the same kilometre rate but add a flat night surcharge of EUR 5. Let $d>0$ be the distance in kilometres. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: The daytime bill for distance $d$ is exactly $12+0.8d$ euros.
If the same distance were run at night, the night bill would be exactly EUR 5 more than the daytime bill for every $d>0$.
There is a distance $d^{*}$ at which a daytime run and a night run would cost the same; solving $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$ finds it.
If the firm waived the EUR 12 base on daytime runs only (charging pure $0.8d$), then for a $20$ km daytime job the client would save exactly EUR 12 compared with the original daytime tariff.
If distance doubled from $10$ km to $20$ km on a daytime run, the bill would also double, because both the base and the kilometre charge scale linearly with $d$.
math.solution_overview:
Day and night courier tariffs are affine in distance $d>0$. Night keeps the same kilometre rate and adds a flat surcharge, so the two cost graphs are parallel vertical translates.

**Part 1: Setup — the two tariffs.**

Daytime base fee (euros):

$$
12
$$

Daytime kilometre rate (euros per km):

$$
0.8
$$

Night flat surcharge (euros):

$$
5
$$

Daytime cost:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

Night cost starts from the day formula and adds the surcharge:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=12+0.8d+5
$$

$$
12+5=17
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=17+0.8d
$$

Same slope on both:

$$
\frac{d}{dd}C_{\mathrm{day}}=0.8
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dd}C_{\mathrm{night}}=0.8
$$

Constant vertical gap:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5
$$

**Part 2: Shared numerical evaluations.**

Kilometre charge at $d=5$:

$$
0.8\times 5=4
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(5)=12+4=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(5)=17+4=21
$$

Kilometre charge at $d=10$:

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(10)=17+8=25
$$

Kilometre charge at $d=20$:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(20)=17+16=33
$$

Waived-base daytime charge at $d=20$:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

Saving versus original daytime bill:

$$
28-16=12
$$

**Part 3: Break-even and doubling checks.**

Set day equal to night:

$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5
$$

$$
0=5
$$

Contradiction, so no break-even $d^{*}$. Doubling $10\to 20$:

$$
\frac{C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)}{C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)}=\frac{28}{20}=1.4
$$

$$
1.4\neq 2
$$

so the bill does not double with distance.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Daytime base EUR $12$ plus EUR $0.8$ per kilometre:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

That is exactly the claimed daytime bill.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Night keeps the same kilometre rate and adds a flat EUR $5$:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=12+0.8d+5=17+0.8d
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5
$$

for every $d>0$. The night bill is exactly EUR $5$ more.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Set day equal to night:

$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 0=5
$$

Contradiction. The two parallel tariffs never meet, so no such $d^{*}$ exists.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Original daytime bill at $d=20$:

$$
12+0.8\cdot 20=12+16=28
$$

Waived-base charge:

$$
0.8\cdot 20=16
$$

$$
28-16=12
$$

The client saves exactly EUR $12$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Daytime bills at the two distances:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+0.8\cdot 10=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+0.8\cdot 20=28
$$

$$
\dfrac{28}{20}=1.4\neq 2
$$

The fixed EUR $12$ base does not scale with $d$, so doubling distance multiplies the bill by $1.4$, not by $2$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Cubic over quadratic — limits and roots
math.context:
Let
$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0,
$$
be a real cubic, and define
$$
s(x)=\dfrac{r(x)}{x^{2}+4}.
$$
Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}s(x)=+\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}r(x)=-\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
If $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, then $(x-2)^{2}$ divides $r(x)$, so $x=2$ is at least a double root.
For every choice of $a,b,c,d$ with $a\neq 0$, the horizontal line $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote of $s$.
If $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=0$, $d=0$, then $r(x)=3x^{2}(x-2)$, so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=2$ is a simple root.
math.solution_overview:
A real cubic $r$ sits over the always-positive quadratic denominator $x^{2}+4$. Asymptotics of the quotient $s=r/(x^{2}+4)$ follow from degree comparison; multiple roots of $r$ follow from shared zeros with $r'$.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0
$$

$$
s(x)=\frac{r(x)}{x^{2}+4}
$$

Degree of the numerator:

$$
\deg r=3
$$

Degree of the denominator:

$$
\deg(x^{2}+4)=2
$$

Compare:

$$
3>2
$$

Derivative of the cubic:

$$
r'(x)=3ax^{2}+2bx+c
$$

**Part 2: Asymptotic rewrite of $s$.**

Factor $ax^{3}$ from the numerator and $x^{2}$ from the denominator:

$$
s(x)=\frac{ax^{3}\bigl(1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\bigr)}{x^{2}\bigl(1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}\bigr)}
$$

Leading ratio:

$$
\frac{ax^{3}}{x^{2}}=ax
$$

$$
s(x)=ax\cdot\frac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

As $|x|\to\infty$ each of $\frac{b}{ax}$, $\frac{c}{ax^{2}}$, $\frac{d}{ax^{3}}$, $\frac{4}{x^{2}}$ tends to $0$, so the fraction tends to $1$ and

$$
s(x)\sim ax
$$

In particular $|s(x)|\to\infty$, so $y=0$ cannot be a horizontal asymptote.

**Part 3: Multiple roots and the concrete example.**

If $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, then $(x-2)^{2}$ divides $r(x)$. For $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=0$, $d=0$:

$$
r(x)=3x^{3}-6x^{2}
$$

$$
3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{2}(x-2)
$$

Check by expanding:

$$
3x^{2}\cdot x=3x^{3}
$$

$$
3x^{2}\cdot(-2)=-6x^{2}
$$

$$
3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{3}-6x^{2}
$$

so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=2$ is a simple root.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Rewrite the quotient by factoring the leading powers:

$$
s(x)=\dfrac{ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d}{x^{2}+4}=ax\cdot\dfrac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

As $x\to+\infty$ the fraction tends to $1$, so $s(x)\sim ax$. Whenever $a>0$ one therefore has

$$
\lim_{x\to+\infty}s(x)=+\infty
$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A cubic with positive leading coefficient tends to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$:

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+\cdots\sim ax^{3}\to-\infty\qquad(a>0,\ x\to-\infty)
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

If $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, then $x=2$ is a root of both $r$ and $r'$. For a polynomial that forces multiplicity at least two, so $(x-2)^{2}$ divides $r(x)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

From letter A, $s(x)\sim ax$ with $a\neq 0$. In particular

$$
|s(x)|\to\infty\qquad\text{as }|x|\to\infty
$$

A horizontal asymptote $y=0$ would require $s(x)\to 0$ at infinity. That never happens for a cubic-over-quadratic with nonzero leading coefficient, so $y=0$ is not a horizontal asymptote for every such choice of coefficients.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

With $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=d=0$:

$$
r(x)=3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{2}(x-2)
$$

The factor $x^{2}$ gives a double root at $x=0$; the factor $(x-2)$ gives a simple root at $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Entangled exponential–log pair — hard compare
math.context:
Define the entangled pair
$$
f(t)=4e^{0.3t},\qquad g(t)=16e^{-0.6t}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}),
$$
and the log-gap
$$
h(t)=\ln f(t)-\ln g(t)=\ln\!\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr).
$$
Also write $p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $f(t)=g(t)$ has the unique real solution $t=\dfrac{1}{0.9}\ln 4=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}$.
$h(t)=\ln 4+0.9t$ for every real $t$, so $h$ is affine with positive slope $0.9$.
If $t$ increases by $\dfrac{10}{3}$, then $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ is multiplied by $e^{-2}$.
The product $p(t)=f(t)g(t)$ is minimized over $\mathbb{R}$ at the same $t$ where $f=g$, and that minimum value equals $64$.
Because $f(0)=4<16=g(0)$ and $f$ grows while $g$ decays, one has $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$.
math.solution_overview:
Two exponential trajectories and the log-gap between them. Every letter follows from the closed forms derived below.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
f(t)=4e^{0.3t}
$$

$$
g(t)=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr)
$$

$$
p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)
$$

**Part 2: Ratio, log-gap, and product — every factor.**

Form the ratio:

$$
\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{4e^{0.3t}}{16e^{-0.6t}}
$$

Constant prefactor:

$$
\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}=0.25
$$

Exponential exponent:

$$
0.3t-(-0.6t)=0.3t+0.6t
$$

$$
0.3+0.6=0.9
$$

$$
\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}
$$

Log-gap:

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}\Bigr)
$$

$$
\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)+\ln(e^{0.9t})
$$

$$
\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)=-\ln 4
$$

$$
\ln 4=\ln(2^{2})=2\ln 2
$$

$$
\ln 2\approx 0.693147
$$

$$
2\times 0.693147=1.386294
$$

$$
\ln 4\approx 1.386294
$$

$$
\ln(e^{0.9t})=0.9t
$$

$$
h(t)=-\ln 4+0.9t
$$

Product:

$$
p(t)=4e^{0.3t}\cdot 16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
4\times 16=64
$$

$$
0.3t+(-0.6t)=-0.3t
$$

$$
p(t)=64e^{-0.3t}
$$

**Part 3: Crossing point.**

Set $f=g$:

$$
4e^{0.3t}=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
\frac{4}{16}e^{0.9t}=1
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}=1
$$

$$
e^{0.9t}=4
$$

$$
0.9t=\ln 4
$$

$$
t=\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}
$$

$$
\frac{1.386294}{0.9}\approx 1.540327
$$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Set $f=g$:

$$
4e^{0.3t}=16e^{-0.6t}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\dfrac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}=1\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad e^{0.9t}=4
$$

$$
t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}
$$

The exponential is one-to-one, so the real solution is unique.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$
\dfrac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\dfrac{4e^{0.3t}}{16e^{-0.6t}}=\dfrac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\dfrac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}\Bigr)=-\ln 4+0.9t
$$

not $\ln 4+0.9t$. The constant term has the wrong sign.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Raise $t$ by $\tfrac{10}{3}$ inside each exponential:

$$
f\Bigl(t+\dfrac{10}{3}\Bigr)=4e^{0.3t}\,e^{0.3\cdot\frac{10}{3}}=f(t)\,e^{1}=e\,f(t)
$$

$$
g\Bigl(t+\dfrac{10}{3}\Bigr)=16e^{-0.6t}\,e^{-0.6\cdot\frac{10}{3}}=g(t)\,e^{-2}
$$

So $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ by $e^{-2}$, exactly as claimed.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Form the product explicitly:

$$
p(t)=4e^{0.3t}\cdot 16e^{-0.6t}=64e^{-0.3t}
$$

Because the exponent $-0.3t$ is strictly decreasing in $t$, so is $p$. A strictly decreasing positive function on $\mathbb{R}$ has no minimum: as $t\to+\infty$, $p(t)\to 0$, and as $t\to-\infty$, $p(t)\to+\infty$.

The crossing point where $f=g$ (letter A) is irrelevant to minimizing $p$. The constant $64$ is simply $p(0)$, not a global minimum value.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

At $t=0$ one has $f(0)=4<16=g(0)$, but letter A shows they meet at $t=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}\approx 1.54>0$. For every larger $t$, $f>g$. So it is false that $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Tangled revenue path — marginal analysis
math.context: A firm faces inverse demand $P(q)=90-3q$ for $0\le q\le 30$ (price in euros, quantity in thousands of units). Revenue is $R(q)=q\cdot P(q)$. Marginal revenue means $R'(q)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $R'(q)=90-6q$, so in particular $R'(4)=66$.
Revenue is maximised at the same quantity where $P(q)=0$, i.e. at the choke quantity $q=30$.
If output rises from $q=4$ to $q=5$, the linear approximation using $R'(4)$ overestimates the true revenue increase $R(5)-R(4)$, because $R$ is a concave quadratic.
At the quantity that maximises $R$, price equals marginal revenue.
Cutting price enough to raise quantity from $q=16$ to $q=17$ must raise revenue, because more units are sold.
math.solution_overview:
Linear inverse demand produces a concave quadratic revenue path. Marginal revenue is the derivative; the revenue peak is where that derivative vanishes.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
P(q)=90-3q,\qquad 0\le q\le 30
$$

$$
R(q)=q\cdot P(q)
$$

$$
R(q)=q(90-3q)
$$

$$
q\cdot 90=90q
$$

$$
q\cdot(-3q)=-3q^{2}
$$

$$
R(q)=90q-3q^{2}
$$

**Part 2: Marginal revenue and the peak.**

Differentiate term by term:

$$
\frac{d}{dq}(90q)=90
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dq}(-3q^{2})=-6q
$$

$$
R'(q)=90-6q
$$

Second derivative:

$$
R''(q)=-6
$$

$$
-6<0
$$

so $R$ is strictly concave. Set marginal revenue to zero:

$$
90-6q=0
$$

$$
6q=90
$$

$$
q=\frac{90}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{90}{6}=15
$$

$$
q^{*}=15
$$

**Part 3: Values at key quantities.**

At the peak $q=15$:

$$
3\times 15=45
$$

$$
P(15)=90-45=45
$$

$$
6\times 15=90
$$

$$
R'(15)=90-90=0
$$

$$
15^{2}=225
$$

$$
90\times 15=1350
$$

$$
3\times 225=675
$$

$$
R(15)=1350-675=675
$$

At the choke quantity $q=30$:

$$
3\times 30=90
$$

$$
P(30)=90-90=0
$$

$$
R(30)=30\times 0=0
$$

At $q=4$ and $q=5$ (used in letter C):

$$
R(4)=360-48=312
$$

$$
R(5)=450-75=375
$$

$$
R(5)-R(4)=63
$$

$$
R'(4)=66
$$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$
R(q)=q(90-3q)=90q-3q^{2}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad R'(q)=90-6q
$$

$$
R'(4)=90-24=66
$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Revenue $R(q)=90q-3q^{2}$ is maximised where marginal revenue vanishes:

$$
R'(q)=90-6q=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad q=15
$$

At the choke quantity $q=30$ one has $P(30)=0$ and therefore $R(30)=0$. That is the right-hand endpoint of the domain, where revenue has fallen back to zero — a minimum on $[0,30]$, not the maximum. The peak is at $q=15$, not at choke.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Evaluate revenue at the two neighbouring outputs:

$$
R(4)=90\cdot 4-3\cdot 16=360-48=312
$$

$$
R(5)=90\cdot 5-3\cdot 25=450-75=375
$$

$$
R(5)-R(4)=63,\qquad R'(4)=90-24=66
$$

The linear step of size $66$ overestimates the true increase $63$. That is the expected bias for a concave quadratic: $R''(q)=-6<0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At the revenue maximum $q=15$:

$$
P(15)=90-3\cdot 15=45,\qquad R'(15)=0
$$

Price is $45$, marginal revenue is $0$; they are not equal.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Past the peak $q=15$, marginal revenue is negative. In particular

$$
R'(16)=90-96=-6<0
$$

so raising quantity from $16$ to $17$ lowers revenue. Selling more units does not raise revenue once one is on the falling side of $R$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: A Positive Test in a Deer Population
math.context: In a wild deer population, 60% are Subspecies A, 25% are Subspecies B, and 15% are Subspecies C. A certain prion disease is present in 2% of Subspecies A, 6% of Subspecies B, and 15% of Subspecies C. A field test for the disease has a 90% sensitivity (probability of a positive result if the deer truly has the disease) and a 4% false-positive rate (probability of a positive result if the deer does not have the disease), regardless of subspecies. A randomly tested deer receives a POSITIVE result.
statements: The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result is greater than 7%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result is greater than 3.4%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive result is greater than 45%.
The probability that a tested deer receives a negative result equals 1 minus the probability that a tested deer receives a positive result.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies C, given a positive result is greater than the probability that the deer is Subspecies B, given a positive result.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For each subspecies, the positive rate mixes sensitivity and the false-positive rate:

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_i)=0.90\cdot P(D\mid S_i)+0.04\cdot P(D^{c}\mid S_i)
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_A)=0.90\cdot 0.02+0.04\cdot 0.98=0.018+0.0392=0.0572
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_B)=0.90\cdot 0.06+0.04\cdot 0.94=0.054+0.0376=0.0916
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_C)=0.90\cdot 0.15+0.04\cdot 0.85=0.135+0.034=0.169
$$

Law of total probability with the subspecies priors:

$$
P(T^{+})=0.0572\cdot 0.60+0.0916\cdot 0.25+0.169\cdot 0.15
$$

$$
=0.03432+0.0229+0.02535=0.08257>0.07
$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$
P(S_A\cap T^{+})=P(T^{+}\mid S_A)P(S_A)=0.0572\cdot 0.60=0.03432>0.034
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Using the joints from letters A and B:

$$
P(S_A\mid T^{+})=\dfrac{0.03432}{0.08257}\approx 0.4156
$$

About $41.6\%$, which is not greater than $45\%$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A tested deer either receives a positive result or a negative result; the two outcomes partition the sample space. Therefore

$$
P(T^{-})=1-P(T^{+})
$$

exactly.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Joints with a positive result:

$$
P(S_B\cap T^{+})=0.0916\cdot 0.25=0.0229
$$

$$
P(S_C\cap T^{+})=0.169\cdot 0.15=0.02535
$$

Divide by the marginal $P(T^{+})=0.08257$ from letter A:

$$
P(S_B\mid T^{+})=\dfrac{0.0229}{0.08257}\approx 0.277
$$

$$
P(S_C\mid T^{+})=\dfrac{0.02535}{0.08257}\approx 0.307
$$

Since $0.307>0.277$, subspecies C is more likely than B given a positive result.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
A randomly tested deer from a three-subspecies population returns a positive field-test result. Every letter reuses the subspecies-conditional positive rates and the law-of-total-probability marginal derived below.

**Part 1: Priors and prevalences.**

$$
P(S_A)=0.60
$$

$$
P(S_B)=0.25
$$

$$
P(S_C)=0.15
$$

$$
P(D\mid S_A)=0.02
$$

$$
P(D\mid S_B)=0.06
$$

$$
P(D\mid S_C)=0.15
$$

Disease-free complements:

$$
1-0.02=0.98
$$

$$
P(D^{c}\mid S_A)=0.98
$$

$$
1-0.06=0.94
$$

$$
P(D^{c}\mid S_B)=0.94
$$

$$
1-0.15=0.85
$$

$$
P(D^{c}\mid S_C)=0.85
$$

Test characteristics:

$$
P(T^{+}\mid D)=0.90
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid D^{c})=0.04
$$

**Part 2: Subspecies-conditional positive rates — every product.**

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_i)=0.90\cdot P(D\mid S_i)+0.04\cdot P(D^{c}\mid S_i)
$$

Subspecies A:

$$
0.90\times 0.02=0.018
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.98=0.0392
$$

$$
0.018+0.0392=0.0572
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_A)=0.0572
$$

Subspecies B:

$$
0.90\times 0.06=0.054
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.94=0.0376
$$

$$
0.054+0.0376=0.0916
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_B)=0.0916
$$

Subspecies C:

$$
0.90\times 0.15=0.135
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.85=0.034
$$

$$
0.135+0.034=0.169
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_C)=0.169
$$

**Part 3: Marginal $P(T^{+})$ and joints.**

$$
0.0572\times 0.60=0.03432
$$

$$
0.0916\times 0.25=0.0229
$$

$$
0.169\times 0.15=0.02535
$$

$$
0.03432+0.0229=0.05722
$$

$$
0.05722+0.02535=0.08257
$$

$$
P(T^{+})=0.08257
$$

$$
P(S_A\cap T^{+})=0.03432
$$

$$
P(S_B\cap T^{+})=0.0229
$$

$$
P(S_C\cap T^{+})=0.02535
$$

$$
P(S_A\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.03432}{0.08257}\approx 0.4156
$$

$$
P(S_B\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.0229}{0.08257}\approx 0.2773
$$

$$
P(S_C\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.02535}{0.08257}\approx 0.3070
$$

math.title: Harbor Foghorn Tests
math.context: Harbor staff run 14 independent foghorn tests. The expected number of clear audible tests is 11.2. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The next test fails with probability 0.2.
The expected number of audible tests in the next 12 tests is 4.8.
The variance of the number of audible tests out of 50 tests is 8.
The probability of 3 consecutive audible tests is less than 0.3.
The probability of at most 4 audible tests in the next 6 tests is more than 0.5.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The stem gives $n=14$ independent tests with expected audible count $11.2$:

$$
p=\dfrac{11.2}{14}=0.8
$$

Failure probability on the next independent test:

$$
1-p=0.2
$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

With $p=0.8$ from letter A, the expected audible count in $12$ tests is

$$
12\cdot 0.8=9.6
$$

not $4.8$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Variance of a binomial count over $50$ tests:

$$
\mathrm{Var}=50\cdot p\cdot(1-p)=50\cdot 0.8\cdot 0.2=8
$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Three independent audible successes:

$$
(0.8)^{3}=0.512
$$

$$
0.512\nless 0.3
$$

The probability is $0.512$, which is not less than $0.3$.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Harbor staff run independent foghorn tests whose clear-audible outcomes form a binomial count. The stem supplies the mean over a block of $14$ trials; every letter reuses the recovered success probability $p=0.8$.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)
$$

Stem data:

$$
n=14
$$

$$
E[X]=11.2
$$

Mean and variance identities:

$$
E[X]=np
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)
$$

**Part 2: Recover $p$ by division.**

$$
p=\frac{E[X]}{n}=\frac{11.2}{14}
$$

$$
14\times 0.8=11.2
$$

$$
\frac{11.2}{14}=0.8
$$

$$
p=0.8
$$

$$
1-p=1-0.8
$$

$$
1-0.8=0.2
$$

$$
1-p=0.2
$$

**Part 3: Shared downstream values.**

Expected audible count in $12$ trials:

$$
12\times 0.8=9.6
$$

Variance in $50$ trials:

$$
50\times 0.8=40
$$

$$
40\times 0.2=8
$$

Three consecutive successes — build the cube:

$$
0.8\times 0.8=0.64
$$

$$
0.64\times 0.8=0.512
$$

$$
(0.8)^{3}=0.512
$$

Lower tail for $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(6,0.8)$:

$$
P(X\le 4)=\sum_{x=0}^{4}\binom{6}{x}(0.8)^{x}(0.2)^{6-x}=0.34464
$$

which is less than $0.5$ (full expansion in letter E).
